title: Deferral of army service for yeshiva students agreed (about 400 students)
summary: In 1948 Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion approved a request from Agudat Yisrael to exempt about 400 full-time yeshiva students from military service, following a pre-state order by Haganah chief of staff Yisrael Galili not to conscript yeshiva students on approved lists. It was justified at the time by the need to restore the Torah world destroyed in the Holocaust, and Ben-Gurion believed the number would diminish. The arrangement began as a quota of roughly 400 deferrals a year and was later widened by administrative decisions (Shimon Peres and yeshiva heads in 1958, an 800-per-year cap after 1967, and the removal of limits by the Begin government in 1977). In a 1958 reply to Rabbi Herzog, who defended yeshiva students as also being enlisted in safeguarding Israel's religion and heritage, Ben-Gurion argued it was first of all a moral issue whether one mother's son should be killed defending the homeland while another studies in safety.

title: Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel
summary: David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel at the Tel Aviv Museum hours before the British Mandate ended. The United States extended de facto recognition that night and the Soviet Union recognised the state three days later. For Palestinian Arabs the period is remembered as the Nakba; fighting that had begun after the UN partition vote of November 1947 now became an interstate war.

title: Palestinian displacement of 1947-1949 (the Nakba)
summary: Between late 1947 and 1949 most Palestinian Arabs in the territory that became Israel fled or were expelled; the UN describes the result as the permanent displacement of more than half of the Palestinian population. Contemporary estimates of the number of refugees include 472,000 (UN Mediator, 1948), about 711,000 from Israel-controlled territory (statistical expert of the UN Conciliation Commission, 1950) and about 750,000 Palestine refugees whom UNRWA served when it began operations in 1950. Israel made any repatriation conditional on a formal peace settlement, and the refugees and their descendants became UNRWA's caseload.

title: Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
summary: In Israel's early years, over 1,000 immigrant families - mostly from Yemen, with dozens from the Balkans, North Africa and other Middle Eastern countries - say their infants and children were taken from hospitals and immigrant camps and given for adoption, sometimes abroad, after the parents were told the children had died. Three state inquiries (a 1967 committee, the Shalgi Commission established in 1988, and the Cohen-Kedmi commission of 1995-2001) found that most of the children had died of disease and were buried without their families being informed; the 2001 report found no systematic state effort, but 69 children disappeared without a trace and it said some may have been handed over for adoption by individual social workers. Families and advocacy groups such as the Amram Association argue the cases reflected policy at the time. On 28 December 2016 the government opened a database of declassified documents (about 200,000 pages per JTA; 400,000 per the Times of Israel), and on 22 February 2021 the cabinet expressed regret and approved NIS 162 million in compensation, without an official apology.

dozens of families from the Balkans also affected (ToI 2021; Al Jazeera)

title: Arab states' armies enter the former Mandate territory
summary: The day after the declaration, forces of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the former Mandate territory; Transjordan's Arab Legion operated mainly in areas allotted to the Arab state and in the Jerusalem zone. For the whole 1948-49 war, the Jewish Virtual Library's casualty table gives 6,373 Israelis killed and an estimated 10,000 Arabs killed, a combined estimate for Palestinians and the Arab armies.

title: Battles of Latrun: Israeli attacks on the Arab Legion fort fail
summary: After the British withdrew in mid-May 1948, Jordan's Arab Legion took the Latrun fort that overlooks the road from the coastal plain to Jerusalem; Israeli sources describe this as strengthening a siege of Jerusalem's roughly 100,000 Jews. Israeli accounts say Ben-Gurion regarded capturing Latrun as the key to liberating Jerusalem. The first assault (Operation Bin Nun Alef, 24-25 May) and a second on 1 June (Bin Nun Bet) failed with heavy Israeli losses, including recent immigrants and Holocaust survivors who had arrived days earlier; three later attacks also failed. The Jewish Virtual Library gives an official Israeli casualty figure of 139 for both main battles, while another source puts the first attack alone at about 75 killed. Israel instead opened the Burma Road bypass, whose first convoy left on 1 June and which could take full-size trucks by 10 June. Latrun stayed in Jordanian hands until the Six-Day War in June 1967.

title: Jewish Quarter of the Old City surrenders to the Arab Legion
summary: On 28 May 1948 the besieged defenders of the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City surrendered to Jordan's Arab Legion; a Truce Commission telegram put the unconditional surrender at 6 p.m. Israel National News says the remaining 1,600 residents were gathered in Batei Machseh Square, about 1,300 women, children and elderly were evacuated to Jewish-held Jerusalem and close to 300 males were taken prisoner; the US vice consul's telegram of 29 May recorded surrender terms of about 2,000 evacuees under Red Cross supervision and 300 men of military age taken prisoner. A UN representative present told the US consulate the Arab Legion had carried out the evacuation efficiently and according to the agreement, while a Jewish Agency official said Arab irregulars on the walls fired on the armoured buses carrying evacuees.

title: The Altalena affair
summary: The Irgun ship Altalena arrived during the truce carrying about 940 volunteers and a large arms cargo. Accounts of the arms talks differ: Lapidot (JVL) writes that Ben-Gurion accepted Begin's request that 20% of the arms go to the Jerusalem Battalion and the two sides deadlocked over the rest, while a World Jewish Congress account says Ben-Gurion rejected the Irgun's demand to retain 20%, insisting there could only be one army. The government ordered the IDF to take the ship, and it was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on 22 June. Sixteen Irgun fighters and three IDF soldiers were killed; Begin ordered his men not to retaliate, and the Irgun was disbanded into the IDF.

title: Operation Dani and the expulsion from Lydda and Ramle
summary: In the 'Ten Days' between the truces, Operation Dani captured Lydda, Ramle and the airfield. On 12-13 July the remaining inhabitants were expelled toward Arab Legion lines: the Institute for Palestine Studies puts the number at about 70,000 including neighbouring villages; many died of thirst and exhaustion on the march. Palestinian sources put those killed inside Lydda at more than 400, including at the Dahmash mosque, and the total including deaths on the march at close to 1,000. An unspecified number of Israeli soldiers were also killed in the capture of Lydda.

title: Al-Dawayima massacre
summary: On 29 October 1948, during Operation Yoav, Israeli troops (8th Brigade; Zochrot names the 89th Battalion) captured al-Dawayima, a Palestinian Arab village about 18 km west of Hebron, and killed civilians there; Israeli and Palestinian accounts say there was no resistance. Estimates of the dead range from 80-100 (an Israeli soldier's account quoted by Benny Morris) to roughly 145 bodies counted by the village mukhtar, who also listed 455 people missing; Morris later spoke of 'hundreds'. The killings caused mass flight of the village's Palestinian residents and refugees sheltering there (4,300 residents per Zochrot; 6,000 plus about 4,000 refugees per the Arab Refugee Congress). Israel told the UN Security Council on 8 November 1948 that the village had been abandoned before its capture; internal Israeli investigations ended with some soldiers disciplined and their findings were not published.

displacement.note: Zochrot: 1948 population 4,300; Arab Refugee Congress (UNCCP Com.Tech/W.3, 1949): population 6,000 plus some 4,000 refugees sheltering there

title: Lausanne Conference of the UN Conciliation Commission (Israel and the Arab states)
summary: From 27 April 1949 the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine met separate Israeli and Arab delegations in Lausanne. On 12 May 1949 it obtained from Israel and the Arab delegations (separately but identically) a Protocol taking a map of the 1947 partition plan as a basis for discussion; the Arabs claimed this amounted to Israeli recognition of the Partition Plan, while Israel held the map was 'a, and not the, basis' for negotiations. The Arab delegations insisted that Israel first accept the principle of repatriation of refugees set out in General Assembly resolution 194, and proposed the immediate return of refugees from territories under Israeli authority that formed part of the Arab zone on the map; Israel said it would accept as citizens the whole Arab population of the Gaza area, including refugees, if Gaza were incorporated into Israel, but declined to propose refugee numbers otherwise. The Commission's 12 September meeting with the Israeli delegation was the last before it adjourned, and UNISPAL summarises it as a lack of progress on the refugee and territorial issues.

title: Negev Bedouin concentrated in the Siyag
summary: After the 1948 war only about 11,000 of an estimated 65,000-95,000 Negev Bedouin remained, according to Human Rights Watch. Much of the land they left was later registered as state land, and Israeli historians cited by HRW say around 50 Jewish settlements were built in that area in the early 1950s.

title: Sinai Campaign (Suez War)
summary: Under the secret Sèvres protocol with Britain and France, Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October 1956; Britain and France issued an ultimatum and attacked the Canal Zone. Israel took Gaza and all of Sinai to Sharm el-Sheikh within days; a ceasefire took effect on 7-8 November under UN General Assembly resolutions. Israeli dead are given as 172 (AP) to 189 (EBSCO); Egyptian dead are estimated at roughly 1,000 to 3,000; British and French dead numbered 82 (AP). During the occupation of the Gaza Strip, UNRWA received lists naming 275 people allegedly killed in Khan Yunis on 3 November and 111 at Rafah camp on 12 November; Israel stated there had been resistance, which refugees denied.

cite.claim: secret Sèvres protocol with Britain and France
cite.quote: On 24 October 1956, in a private villa in Sèvres on the outskirts of Paris, representatives of the British, French, and Israeli governments, at the end of a three-day meeting which was concealed behind a thick veil of secrecy, signed a most curious document which later came to be known as the Protocol of Sèvres.

cite.claim: date 1956-10-29: Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October 1956
cite.quote: The Israeli forces crossed the border on the morning of 29 October.

cite.claim: Britain and France issued an ultimatum
cite.quote: In the afternoon of the same day, the British and French Governments addressed a joint ultimatum to Egypt and Israel calling on both sides to cease hostilities within 12 hours and to withdraw their forces to a distance of 10 miles on each side of the Suez Canal.

cite.claim: Britain and France attacked the Canal Zone (place: suez_canal)
cite.quote: Later in the day, the British representative announced that a ceasefire had been ordered at Port Said. ... On 22 December, the withdrawal of the Anglo-French forces was completed and UNEF took over the Port Said area.

cite.claim: Israel took all of Sinai to Sharm el-Sheikh within days (places: sinai, sharm_el_sheikh)
cite.quote: Date: October 29-November 6, 1956 Location: Sinai Desert ... Result: Israeli conquest of the Sinai ... Sharp battles took place at Thamad, Abu Ageila, and Sharm el-Sheikh, but the issue was never in doubt.

cite.claim: Israel took the Gaza Strip, incl. Khan Yunis (3 Nov) and Rafah (places: gaza_strip, khan_yunis, rafah)
cite.quote: The town of Khan Yunis and the Agency's camp adjacent thereto were occupied by Israel troops on the morning of 3 November.

cite.claim: ceasefire took effect on 7-8 November under UN General Assembly resolutions
cite.quote: The ceasefire was established at midnight GMT on 7/8 November and, except for isolated incidents, generally held.

cite.claim: Israeli dead 172 (AP)
cite.quote: ISRAEL’S SINAI CAMPAIGN, 1956: Israel lost 172 killed, 817 wounded.

cite.claim: Israeli dead 189 (EBSCO)
cite.quote: Total casualties amounted to 189 killed, 899 wounded for Israel, versus an estimated 1,030 killed and 4,000 wounded for Egypt.

cite.claim: Egyptian dead roughly 1,000 to 3,000
cite.quote: Egyptian casualties were an estimated 2,000-3,000 dead.

cite.claim: neutrality: summary/casualties omit Palestinian civilians killed in the Gaza Strip during the occupation (Khan Yunis, Rafah)
cite.quote: the Director has received from sources he considers trustworthy lists of names of persons allegedly killed on 3 November, numbering 275 individuals, of whom 140 were refugees and 135 local residents of Khan Yunis. ... lists of names of persons allegedly killed at Rafah on 12 November, numbering 111, of whom 103 were refugees, seven local residents, and one an Egyptian.
cite.page: UN doc A/3212/Add.1 (UNRWA Director's special report), 15 Dec 1956

cite.claim: neutrality: casualties omit British and French dead
cite.quote: British and French casualties in the invasion of Suez, which coincided with Israel’s thrust into the Sinai desert, were 82 killed and 129 wounded.

cite.claim: choice 1 (historical): Ben-Gurion, Dayan and Peres agreed the Sèvres protocol of 22-24 October 1956
cite.quote: The senior members of the Israeli delegation to the talks in Paris were David Ben-Gurion, who was defence minister as well as prime minister, Moshe Dayan, the IDF chief of staff, and Shimon Peres, the director-general of the ministry of defence. ... The results of the conversations which took place at Sèvres from 22-24 October 1956

cite.claim: choice 2: continuing limited reprisal raids without a full war was a genuine pre-war policy (Shlaim)
cite.quote: Two schools of thought were competing for control over policy in the conflict with the Arabs: the school of retaliation and the school of negotiation. ... Ben-Gurion had temporarily dropped the idea of a preventive war against Egypt in the early months of 1956.
cite.page: Avi Shlaim, 'Israel between East and West, 1948-56'

cite.claim: choice 3: 'Seek arms and a security guarantee from France without going to war', associated with Sharett
cite.quote: Sharett’s foreign policy had an American orientation in that he looked to America for political support, a security guarantee, economic aid, and arms. ... Since the alliance with France was predicated on Israel’s willingness to go to war against Egypt, the debate over orientation merged with the other great debate on the question of preventive war.
cite.page: Avi Shlaim, 'Israel between East and West, 1948-56'

cite.claim: UNRWA: 275 allegedly killed at Khan Yunis on 3 Nov 1956
cite.quote: lists of names of persons allegedly killed on 3 November, numbering 275 individuals, of whom 140 were refugees and 135 local residents of Khan Yunis.

cite.claim: UNRWA: 111 allegedly killed at Rafah on 12 Nov 1956
cite.quote: lists of names of persons allegedly killed at Rafah on 12 November, numbering 111, of whom 103 were refugees, seven local residents, and one an Egyptian.

cite.claim: Israeli authorities said there was resistance; refugees deny it
cite.quote: The Israel authorities in Gaza state that the attitude of the refugees in Rafah camp was hostile and that there was some resistance to the screening operation

affected_populations.note: UNRWA name lists of persons allegedly killed at Khan Yunis (275, 3 Nov) and Rafah (111, 12 Nov); UNRWA lists a further 66 in smaller incidents 1-21 Nov. Accounts of the circumstances conflict.
AP.

consequences.note: History took its course: the Sinai war opens on 29 October 1956 on the game's calendar. Your cabinet declined the Sevres collusion, so in your Israel the army goes in alone after the fedayeen raids: no French fighters guard Israeli skies, no Anglo-French landing at the Canal draws off Egypt's army (the Egyptian fronts in Sinai are stronger), and a solo invasion is condemned without Britain and France to share the blame (Standing -7 instead of -5). In history Israel attacked under the secret Sevres protocol.

title: Nazareth Illit (Nof HaGalil) founded

title: Withdrawal from Sinai and Gaza; UNEF deployed
summary: Under US pressure and UN General Assembly resolutions 1124 and 1125 of 2 February 1957, Israel announced on 1 March that it would withdraw. It left the Gaza Strip on 6-7 March and Sharm el-Sheikh on 8-12 March 1957. UNEF deployed along the armistice line and at Sharm el-Sheikh, where a UNEF detachment kept the Strait of Tiran under watch; its stationing there required Egyptian consent. The strait stayed open to Israeli shipping until Egypt closed it in May 1967.

cite.quote: The withdrawal from the Gaza Strip took place on 6 and 7 March 1957 and that from the Sharm el Sheikh area from 8 to 12 March.

cite.quote: Third phase: Gaza Strip and Sharm el Sheikh (March 1957) After 22 January 1957, Israel held on to the last two areas it still occupied.

cite.claim: Withdrawal dates from Gaza and Sharm el-Sheikh
cite.quote: The withdrawal from the Gaza Strip took place on 6 and 7 March 1957 and that from the Sharm el Sheikh area from 8 to 12 March.

cite.claim: UNEF detachment at Sharm el-Sheikh watched the Strait of Tiran

consequences.note: History took its course: Israel leaves Gaza and Sharm el-Sheikh in March 1957 on the game's calendar and UNEF deploys. Your cabinet tried to hold on until guarantees were in hand, so in your Israel the withdrawal comes under the threat of American sanctions rather than on American assurances: the standing gain is small (+1 instead of +4). In history Israel announced the withdrawal on 1 March after US assurances on free passage in the Gulf of Aqaba.

title: Franco-Israeli agreement on the Dimona reactor
summary: France agreed to build a 24-megawatt research reactor near Dimona, constructed in secret outside IAEA inspection. Ben-Gurion acknowledged the reactor publicly in December 1960, describing it as for peaceful purposes, and gave the US assurances to that effect; it went critical in 1964. Israel maintains a policy of nuclear ambiguity.

cite.claim: Ben-Gurion acknowledged the reactor publicly in December 1960, describing it as for peaceful purposes

title: Wadi Salib riots in Haifa
summary: Police shot and wounded Moroccan-born Akiva Elkrif in Wadi Salib, a former Arab quarter of Haifa housing North African immigrants in poor conditions. Protests led by the Union of North African Immigrants spread to other towns and brought discrimination against Mizrahi Jews into national politics.

cite.quote: The protests in Wadi Salib erupted on the night of July 8 after police shot and injured Akiva Yaakov Elkrif, a Moroccan-born migrant.

cite.claim: Wadi Salib a former Arab quarter of Haifa housing North African immigrants in poor conditions (place: haifa)
cite.quote: Wadi Salib, which following the Nakba was transformed from an Arab neighborhood to a Jewish one ... Despite the difficult living conditions and deprivation in Wadi Salib in the 1950s, the area attracted Jewish migrants from Morocco

cite.claim: protests led by the Union of North African Immigrants
cite.quote: Hundreds of residents of the neighborhood, led by the Union of Migrants from North Africa (Irgun Likud ‛Oley Tsfon Afrika), clashed with the police

cite.claim: protests spread to other towns (place: beersheba)
cite.quote: Throughout July, the demonstrations spread to other cities with high concentrations of migrants from Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) countries, particularly Be’er Sheva, Acre, Tiberias, and Migdal HaEmek.

cite.quote: The Etzioni Commission was established by the government on July 19, 1959 to investigate the causes of the outbreak of demonstrations ... The Moroccan-Jewish protest in Wadi Salib, the Iraqi-Jewish protest in the transit camps (ma‛abarot) in the early 1950s, and the Black Panthers protest movement ... became emblematic of Mizrahi protests in Israel.

summary: Mossad agents seized Adolf Eichmann, a principal organiser of the Holocaust, near his home in Buenos Aires and flew him secretly to Israel; Ben-Gurion announced the capture to the Knesset on 23 May 1960. Argentina protested the violation of its sovereignty at the UN Security Council.

title: Eichmann trial
summary: The trial opened in Jerusalem before a special panel headed by Judge Moshe Landau, with Attorney-General Gideon Hausner prosecuting; testimony from survivors made the Holocaust central to Israeli and world awareness. cite.quote: the Eichmann Trial put survivors at center stage. ... The trial prompted a new openness in Israel; many Holocaust survivors who had heretofore remained silent about their experiences felt able to share their experiences

cite.claim: sentenced to death on 15 December 1961
cite.quote: Seven months later Eichmann was convicted and on December 15 1961 the court sentenced Eichmann to death.

cite.claim: date_end 1962-06-01: hanged on the night of 31 May-1 June 1962
cite.quote: on the night between May 31 and June 1 1962, Adolf Eichmann was executed.

cite.claim: hanged at Ramla (place: ramla)
cite.quote: A few minutes before midnight on May 31, 1962, Eichmann was executed by hanging in Ramleh, Israel.

consequences.note: History took its course: Adolf Eichmann stands trial in 1961 on the game's calendar, but in your Israel before the international tribunal your cabinet asked for, not the Jerusalem District Court. The survivors testify abroad and their words reach Israeli homes less directly (Culture +10 instead of +30), while placing the case under international law earns more standing (+4 instead of +2); Israel does not decide the sentence. In history the trial opened in Jerusalem on 11 April 1961 before Judge Moshe Landau.

title: Mughrabi Quarter of the Old City demolished and residents evicted
summary: On 10 June 1967, days after Israeli forces took the Old City, the Mughrabi (Moroccan) Quarter beside the Western Wall in Jerusalem was cleared and demolished to create the Western Wall plaza. Sources give the number evicted as approximately 650 people (Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs) or 108 families (Israel Hayom); MERIP says more than 100 families were told they had three hours to leave. Mayor Teddy Kollek and army officers gave the order, according to the JCPA; Kollek later wrote that something had to be done about the small slum houses crowding the Wall. The JCPA argues the demolition was justified and necessary for public safety and for tens of thousands of worshippers expected at Shavuot, and says many residents later received compensation; it describes the New Yorker article it answers as calling the demolition a war crime under the Fourth Geneva Convention. French historian Vincent Lemire cites minutes of a 9 June meeting between Kollek and the army commander listing the quarter's destruction as an agenda item, and argues it was premeditated and planned.

title: War of Attrition
summary: Artillery duels and raids along the Suez Canal, under way since 1967, escalated after Nasser declared a war of attrition in March 1969; Israel answered with commando raids and deep air strikes, and Soviet air-defence personnel deployed in Egypt. A US-brokered ceasefire took effect on 7-8 August 1970. Israel counts 1,424 soldiers and more than 100 civilians killed between 15 June 1967 and 8 August 1970; Egyptian deaths are estimated at about 5,000. The main cities on the Egyptian side of the canal were destroyed and about a million inhabitants were evacuated. Egyptian civilians were also killed: Israeli deep-penetration raids in early 1970 hit a factory at Abu Zaabal (89 workers killed) and a school at Bahr el-Baqar (30 children killed, per Egyptian reports; Israel said it had targeted military installations).

title: Black September: Jordan expels the PLO
summary: After the PFLP's Dawson's Field hijackings (6-12 September 1970), the Jordanian army moved against Palestinian guerrilla organisations; a Syrian armoured incursion was turned back and Israel readied forces as Jordan asked Western governments for help. Estimates of Palestinian dead are about 2,000-4,000 fighters plus an unknown number of civilians (Arafat claimed 25,000); Jordan reports that 537 of its soldiers were killed. Syrian casualties are not reliably quantified (a Jordanian commander's account gives 135 Syrian tanks lost and 1,500 casualties; an Israeli assessment gave 120 tanks, some lost to breakdowns). Thousands of Palestinians sought refuge in Syria and Lebanon; fighting ended in July 1971 and the PLO relocated to Lebanon.

title: 1982 Lebanon War (Operation Peace for Galilee)
summary: After the attempted assassination of Ambassador Shlomo Argov in London by the Abu Nidal group, Israel invaded Lebanon on 6 June 1982. The cabinet had approved an operation to push the PLO about 40 km from the border; according to Schiff and Ya'ari, Defence Minister Sharon expanded it step by step, fighting Syrian forces and besieging West Beirut until PLO fighters were evacuated in August-September. Lebanese police figures reported in December 1982 counted 19,085 people killed and 30,302 wounded between 4 June and 31 August 1982, fighters included; in Beirut 84 percent of the 6,775 dead were civilians. Sharon disputed media casualty figures, speaking in late August of some 2,000 civilian casualties. On the Israeli side the army reported 269 soldiers killed in the first 20 days, Sharon gave 350 for the operation, the army counted 446 by 19 November 1982, and Israel Radio's count of Israelis killed in Lebanon reached 478 by May 1983.

cite.quote: Thus he deliberately and continually moved his troops forward, provoking the reluctant Syrians into what he felt was a necessary confrontation and bringing Israeli forces into Beirut

cite.claim: after the attempted assassination of Ambassador Shlomo Argov in London by the Abu Nidal group

Israel launches its "Peace for Galilee" operation in Lebanon which Begin assures Reagan is solely designed to push the PLO out of rocket and artillery range of Israel's northern border settlements. cite.quote: which Begin assures Reagan is solely designed to push the PLO out of rocket and artillery range of Israel's northern border settlements. In two days, Israeli forces cover twice the intended distance of 25 miles

cite.claim: Cabinet thought it approved a 40 km incursion

cite.quote: According to a count kept by Israel Radio, the number of Israelis killed in Lebanon since the start of the war there last June now stands at 478 and 2,614 wounded.

consequences.note: History took its course: the war opens on 6 June 1982 on the game's calendar, three days after the attempt on Ambassador Shlomo Argov's life in London gives the clearer provocation your cabinet had waited for. Because your cabinet held back in the spring, the invasion begins with somewhat less condemnation abroad (Standing -4 instead of -6) but against PLO and Syrian positions that had more months to dig in (stronger fronts).

title: Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel assassinated
summary: Bashir Gemayel, the Phalange leader elected president of Lebanon on 23 August 1982 with Israeli backing, was killed on 14 September 1982 when a bomb destroyed the Phalangist party headquarters in east Beirut; first reports put eight others dead and at least 50 injured. A later JTA account attributed the killing, 'presumably', to the Syrians. The IDF entered West Beirut the next day.

cite.claim: Bashir Gemayel, elected president of Lebanon with Israeli backing, was assassinated (places: beirut, lebanon)
cite.quote: Gemayel, elected president in July, spoke of peace with Israel, telling Israeli leaders that he would "come to Jerusalem as a second Sadat." Two months later he was assassinated, presumably by the Syrians

cite.claim: date 1982-09-14: killed by a bomb at Phalange headquarters
cite.quote: The Report found that when word of Bashir Jemayel's assassination reached Israel at approximately 11:00 P.M. on Tuesday, September 14

cite.claim: the IDF entered West Beirut the next day
cite.quote: Israeli troops enter west Beirut following the assassination of Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel.

cite.claim: killed by a bomb that destroyed the Phalangist headquarters in east Beirut; eight others reported dead and at least 50 injured
cite.quote: Gemayel succumbed to injuries sustained when a massive bomb explosion destroyed the head quarters of his Christian Phalangist Party in east Beirut where he was attending a meeting. Eight other persons were reported dead and at least 50 injured.

cite.claim: elected president on 23 August 1982
cite.quote: Gemayel, the 34-year-old Christian Phalangist leader who was elected August 23 to succeed Elias Sarkis and was to be sworn into office next week,

affected_populations.note: Gemayel and eight others reported dead, at least 50 injured (JTA, 16 Sep 1982 - first reports; no final toll found in an opened source).

title: Sabra and Shatila massacre
summary: Between 16 and 18 September 1982 Lebanese Phalangist militiamen, admitted by the IDF into the Sabra neighbourhood and Shatila refugee camp in Israeli-controlled West Beirut, killed civilians, mainly Palestinians and Lebanese; Iranians, Syrians, Pakistanis and Algerians were also among the dead. Estimates of the toll range from roughly 300 to 3,000: the official Red Cross burial counted 328 bodies; Lebanon's prosecutor general reported 597 bodies found and 2,000 people missing; the IDF estimated 700-800 killed; other estimates put the dead at about 1,000; and one Israeli source put the number of civilians killed at 3,000. The killings caused a political crisis in Israel.

cite.claim: date 16-18 September 1982: Lebanese Phalangist militiamen, admitted by the IDF into Sabra and Shatila in Israeli-controlled West Beirut, killed civilians (places: beirut, lebanon)
cite.quote: On September 16, 1982, the Israeli Defense Forces ("IDF") occupying Beirut as a result of Israel's June invasion of Lebanon per[mitted the Phalangists to enter] ... The Commission of Inquiry focused on the events of September 16-18, 1982, when the massacres occurred.

cite.claim: the killings caused a political crisis in Israel
cite.quote: The Cabinet's action today represented the second reversal by the government on the issue of an inquiry in little more than a week. On September 21 the Cabinet refused to take any action despite mounting calls in Israel and abroad for a judicial inquiry.

cite.claim: victims were mainly Palestinians and Lebanese, also Iranians, Syrians, Pakistanis and Algerians; the Red Cross burial counted 328 bodies
cite.quote: The official Red Cross burial of the dead counted 328 bodies, including Palestinians, Lebanese, Iranians, Syrians, Pakistanis and Algerians.

cite.claim: estimates range from roughly 300 to 3,000
cite.quote: Estimates of those massacred have ranged from roughly 300 to as many as 3000 people.

cite.claim: the IDF estimated 700-800 killed; other estimates about 1,000; one Israeli source 3,000
cite.quote: The IDF estimates 700 to 800 were killed.121 There have been estimates that approximately a thousand were killed122 and over 900 people put into trucks and driven away.123 One Israeli source put the total number of civilians killed at 3000.

cite.claim: Lebanon's prosecutor general reported 597 bodies found and 2,000 people missing
cite.quote: Lebanese Prosecutor General Camille Geagea, heading an investigation, says 597 bodies found, 2,000 people still missing

affected_populations.note: Range of estimates (Malone, Utah L. Rev. 1985): Red Cross burial count 328; IDF 700-800; about 1,000; one Israeli source 3,000. Lebanese prosecutor general (24 Sep 1982): 597 bodies found, 2,000 missing.

consequences.note: Your cabinet halted the army at the 40 km line, so in your Israel the IDF is not in West Beirut in September 1982 and does not admit Phalangist militiamen into the Sabra and Shatila camps: the massacre as it happened, in an area under Israeli control, is not part of your Israel's record, and there is no Kahan inquiry into it. What the Lebanese civil war would have brought instead is not modelled. In history Phalangists killed hundreds of civilians, mainly Palestinians and Lebanese, there on 16-18 September 1982.

History took its course: the army reached Beirut after the invasion of June 1982, and on 16-18 September Phalangist militiamen admitted by the IDF killed civilians in Sabra and Shatila, an area under Israeli control. Your cabinet's restraint in the spring of 1982 does not lessen Israel's share of the responsibility the inquiry will weigh.

title: Mass protest in Tel Aviv demands inquiry
summary: On the night of 25 September 1982 a mass rally in Tel Aviv, organised by the Labor Alignment, the Shinui party and Peace Now, protested the Sabra and Shatila massacre and the government's refusal to set up a full independent inquiry; speakers called for the resignations of Prime Minister Begin and Defence Minister Sharon. Crowd figures were contested: the organisers gave the New York Times a figure of 350,000 and claimed to JTA 'over 400,000', while police declined to give an estimate but called it one of the largest rallies ever held. The government appointed the Kahan Commission days later.

cite.claim: the government appointed the Kahan Commission days later
cite.quote: September 29, 1982 ... The Cabinet decided unanimously today to establish a judicial commission to conduct a full, formal inquiry into the circumstances of the massacre of Palestinian civilians in the Shatila and Sabra refugee camps

cite.claim: organisers told the New York Times the crowd numbered 350,000
cite.quote: Organizers of the rally said the crowd numbered 350,000; the country has a population of about four million.

cite.claim: speakers called for Begin's and Sharon's resignation and an independent judicial inquiry
cite.quote: Rallying in a plaza before City Hall here, the throng gave thunderous roars of applause and cheers to speakers who called on Mr. Begin and his Defense Minister, Ariel Sharon, to resign. Equally raucous eruptions greeted calls for the creation of an independent judicial inquiry commission to assess the Israeli role in the massacre

cite.claim: date 1982-09-25 (Saturday night): rally against the massacre and the refusal to set up an independent inquiry (place: tel_aviv)
cite.quote: Last Saturday night’s rally here to protest the massacre of Palestinians in two refugee camps in west Beirut and the government’s refusal (at that point) to launch a full independent investigation of the carnage was the largest rally ever to have taken place in Israel, either in support of or in opposition to government policies.

cite.claim: organisers (Labor Alignment, Shinui, Peace Now) claimed over 400,000; police gave no estimate
cite.quote: The rally’s organizers — the Labor Alignment; the Shinui Party and the Peace Now movement — claimed that “over 400,000” people participated from all over the country and that the participants crossed party lines. Police declined to give on estimate of attendance, but said it was “one of the largest” rallies to have been held.

cite.claim: speakers called for the resignations of Begin and Sharon
cite.quote: this one, at which speakers also called for the resignations of Premier Menachem Begin and Defense Minister Ariel Sharon,

title: IDF headquarters in Tyre destroyed
summary: An explosion destroyed the Israeli military headquarters in Tyre on 11 November 1982, killing 76 Israeli soldiers, Shin Bet agents and Border Police and 15 Lebanese detainees (IDF figures; counts of the detainees vary). Israel's inquiry at the time attributed the collapse to a gas explosion. A truck bomb at the Israeli headquarters in Tyre on 4 November 1983 killed 29 Israeli service personnel and 31 Lebanese, according to JTA.

cite.claim: date 1982-11-11: an explosion destroyed the Israeli military headquarters in Tyre, killing 76 Israeli soldiers, Shin Bet agents and Border Police and 15 Lebanese detainees (IDF figures) (place: south_lebanon)
cite.quote: the collapse of the administrative building in Tyre, Lebanon on November 11th, 1982 ... 76 members of the Israel security forces (Israel Border Police, IDF and ISA) were killed, as well as 15 Lebanese detainees who were in the building.

cite.claim: earlier counts of detainees varied
cite.quote: the collapse of a seven story building housing the Israeli local military headquarters in Tyre, which kills 90 people, including 76 Israelis and 14 Arabs

cite.claim: Israel's inquiry at the time attributed the collapse to a gas explosion
cite.quote: Within the conclusions it was determined that the disaster occurred as a result of a gas explosion

cite.claim: a truck bomb at the Israeli headquarters in Tyre on 4 November 1983 killed 29 Israeli service personnel and 31 Lebanese
cite.quote: the November 4 truck-bomb attack on Israeli military headquarters in Tyre ... the November 4 bombing in Tyre which took the lives of 29 Israeli service personnel and 31 Lebanese.

affected_populations.note: 76 in 1982 (IDF) and 29 in 1983 (JTA).
1982: 15 (IDF) or 14 (JTA 1983); 1983: 31 Lebanese (JTA).

title: Kahan Commission report
summary: The state commission of inquiry headed by Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan made its report public on 8-9 February 1983. It found Israel indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila killings and Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible for disregarding the danger of bloodshed, and recommended that he resign or be dismissed. The cabinet voted 16-1 to accept the recommendations, Sharon casting the only vote against; he left the defence ministry but remained in the cabinet as minister without portfolio.

cite.claim: the commission headed by Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan found Israel indirectly responsible (place: jerusalem)
cite.quote: Yitzhak Kahan, President of the Israeli Supreme Court and Commission chairman ... concluded that the State of Israel and several individual Israelis, including Ariel Sharon, were "indirectly" responsible

cite.claim: found Defence Minister Sharon personally responsible for disregarding the danger of bloodshed and recommended his removal
cite.quote: We have found ... that the Minister of Defense bears personal responsibility ... it is fitting that the Minister of Defense draw the appropriate personal conclusions ... and if necessary, that the Prime Minister consider whether he should exercise his authority ... to "remove a minister from office."

cite.claim: Sharon left the defence ministry but remained in the cabinet as minister without portfolio
cite.quote: remained in the cabinet but lost his portfolio

cite.claim: date: the report was made public on 8-9 February 1983 (JTA bulletin of 9 February: published 'this morning')
cite.quote: The commission, in its report and recommendations published here this morning, accepted Begin’s testimony that he knew nothing of the massacres until he heard of them from a foreign radio broadcast after the fact.

cite.claim: date: Malone dates the commission's conclusions 9 February 1983
cite.quote: On February 9, 1983, an Israeli commission of inquiry into the massacres concluded that the State of Israel and several individual Israelis, including Ariel Sharon, were "indirectly" responsible for the massacres.

cite.claim: recommended that Sharon resign or be dismissed
cite.quote: The commission recommended that if Sharon does not resign, Premier Menachem Begin should exercise his statutory authority and dismiss him.

cite.claim: the cabinet voted 16-1 to accept the recommendations, Sharon casting the only vote against
cite.quote: The Cabinet voted 16-1 tonight to accept in full the report and recommendations of the commission of inquiry into the Beirut refugee camps massacre. Defense Minister Ariel Sharon, whose resignation was called for by the commission, cast the lone dissenting vote.

consequences.note: With the army held at the 40 km line in your Israel, there was no massacre in Beirut under Israeli control and so no Kahan Commission report in February 1983. In history the commission found Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible for ignoring the danger of bloodshed and he left the Defence Ministry.

title: 17 May Agreement with Lebanon
summary: US-mediated talks produced an agreement on 17 May 1983 ending the state of war between Israel and Lebanon and providing for Israeli withdrawal. Under Syrian pressure Lebanon abrogated it in March 1984.

cite.claim: date 1983-05-17: US-mediated agreement ending the state of war and providing for Israeli withdrawal (places: beirut, lebanon)
cite.quote: Lebanon formerly abrogates its May 17, 1983 withdrawal and security agreement with Israel.

cite.claim: under Syrian pressure Lebanon abrogated it in March 1984
cite.quote: Bitter Reactions in Israel over Lebanon's Formal Abrogation of the May 17 Agreement March 6, 1984

consequences.note: Your cabinet rejected the accord, so there is no 17 May 1983 agreement in your Israel: the state of war with Lebanon is not ended and the army holds its lines in south Lebanon (your choice's lasting terms carry the cost). In history Israel and Lebanon signed it, and Lebanon abrogated it under Syrian pressure in March 1984.

History took its course: the US-mediated agreement with Lebanon is signed on 17 May 1983. With the army held at the 40 km line in your Israel, the accord covers a smaller zone and a quicker withdrawal, so it is less contested at home (no Cohesion cost); its terms, an end to the state of war and a security zone, follow history.

History took its course: the US-mediated agreement with Lebanon is signed on 17 May 1983, after the war that came in June 1982 despite your cabinet's restraint in the spring; its terms follow history.

title: Bank shares crisis
summary: Israel's major banks had for years propped up their own share prices. When the shares began to collapse, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange closed from 6 October 1983 for about two weeks, and the government undertook to buy bank shares from the public, effectively nationalising the main banks. The Bejski Commission reported on the affair in April 1986.

cite.claim: banks had propped up their own share prices; when shares collapsed the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange closed from 6 October 1983 (place: tel_aviv)
cite.quote: Bank shares plummeted in value over the weekend, precipitating panic. The government took measures to shore them up. The sale of bank shares was suspended. The Tel Aviv stock exchange closed Sunday and was expected to remain closed for the rest of the week

cite.claim: the government undertook to buy bank shares from the public, effectively nationalising the main banks (historical choice 'the arrangement')
cite.quote: its earlier decision to shore up sagging commercial bank shares in order to protect tens of thousands of investors ... the bank shares backed by the government would revert to the value they had on October 6 ... They would be linked to the U.S. Dollar and investors who hold them for five y[ears]

cite.claim: the Bejski Commission reported on the affair in April 1986
cite.quote: April 22, 1986 ... a report released Sunday night by the special commission set up to investigate the collapse of bank shares ... The commission, headed by Supreme Court Justice Chaim Beisky

cite.claim: choice (non-historical): let bank share prices fall without a state guarantee — opposed at the time by the Finance Minister
cite.quote: The decision was taken despite strenuous opposition by Finance Minister Y[oram Aridor] ... many ministers who approved it have had second thoughts.

cite.claim: the exchange closed for about two weeks
cite.quote: in October 1983, after the collapse of the bank shares, in the course of which tens of thousands of citizens lost their savings, the government ordered the closing down of the stock market for two weeks.

title: Begin resigns; Yitzhak Shamir becomes Prime Minister
title_he: התפטרות בגין ויצחק שמיר לראשות הממשלה
summary: Menachem Begin, who had withdrawn from public life after his wife's death in November 1982 and amid the protracted Lebanon war, resigned in 1983. Yitzhak Shamir formed the Twentieth Government on 10 October 1983.

cite.claim: Begin had withdrawn after his wife's death in November 1982 and amid the Lebanon war, and resigned in 1983
cite.quote: Begin announced on August 29, 1983, that he planned to resign ... On September 15, he officially submitted his resignation. ... The decision came following the death of his wife, Aliza, in the winter of 1982 and his despair over the conduct of the war in Lebanon.

cite.claim: date 1983-10-10: Yitzhak Shamir formed the Twentieth Government on 10 October 1983
cite.quote: Government 20 10/10/1983 - 13/09/1984 Ministers Faction ** Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir 10/10/1983 - 13/09/1984 Likud

title: Bus 300 affair
summary: Four Palestinians from the Gaza Strip hijacked an Egged bus on 12 April 1984. In the rescue the next morning an Israeli soldier, Irit Portuguez, was killed and seven passengers were wounded; two hijackers were killed and two captured alive, who were then killed on the orders of Shin Bet chief Avraham Shalom. A press photograph exposed the cover-up; Shalom and other officers received presidential pardons in 1986.

cite.claim: date 1984-04-12: four Palestinians hijacked a bus (Tel Aviv-Ashkelon) on 12 April 1984 (places: tel_aviv, gaza_strip)
cite.quote: the killing of four terrorists who hijacked a Tel Aviv-to-Ashkelon bus on April 12 ... The four terrorists, all residents of the Gaza Strip

cite.claim: in the rescue the next morning two were killed and two captured alive
cite.quote: According to the army, two of the terrorists were killed instantly when troops stormed the bus in the early hours of Friday, April 13 ... an Israeli reporter from the newspaper Hadoshot, who was at the scene, said he saw one of the terrorists, apparently unharmed, being led away from the bus handcuffed

cite.claim: the two captured were killed on the orders of Shin Bet chief Avraham Shalom
cite.quote: the pardons granted by President Chaim Herzog to the head of the Shin Bet intelligence agency, Avraham Shalom, and three Shin Bet officials in the 1984 case in which two Palestinian bus-hijackers were killed in Israeli custody.

cite.claim: a press photograph exposed the cover-up
cite.quote: The reporter took a photograph of the man. According to reports in the Israeli and foreign media, the photograph was readily identified by friends and relatives as Majdi Abu Jama

cite.claim: Shalom and other officers received presidential pardons in 1986
cite.quote: August 7, 1986 ... The High Court of Justice upheld Wednesday the pardons granted by President Chaim Herzog to the head of the Shin Bet intelligence agency, Avraham Shalom, and three Shin Bet officials

cite.claim: neutrality: omits the Israeli soldier killed and passengers wounded
cite.quote: (One Israeli woman soldier, Irit Portuguez, 19, was killed in the shootout and seven passengers were wounded.)

affected_populations.note: Irit Portuguez, 19, killed in the shootout when troops stormed the bus (JTA).
Seven passengers wounded (JTA).
Two killed when the bus was stormed; the two captured alive were then killed on the orders of Shin Bet chief Avraham Shalom (JTA).

title: Jewish Underground uncovered
summary: The Shin Bet arrested members of a settler underground in late April 1984 after they planted bombs on Arab buses in East Jerusalem. The group was responsible for the 1980 car bombings of West Bank mayors and the July 1983 attack on the Islamic College in Hebron that killed three students and wounded about 30-33, and had planned to blow up the Dome of the Rock.

cite.claim: date late April 1984: the security services arrested members of a settler underground after they planted bombs on Arab buses in East Jerusalem (places: jerusalem)
cite.quote: April 30, 1984 ... the attempted mass sabotage of Arab-owned buses in East Jerusalem by what apparently is a well organized gang of Jewish extremists based in the occupied territories. The attempt was foiled early Friday morning when police sappers safely dismantled time bombs planted in six buses ... As of noon today, at least 30 suspects had been ro[unded up]

cite.claim: the group was responsible for the 1980 car bombings of West Bank mayors
cite.quote: the June, 1980 car bombings that maimed two West Bank Arab mayors ... the ongoing investigation of a Jewish terrorist underground

cite.claim: and the July 1983 attack on the Islamic College in Hebron that killed three students (places: hebron, kiryat_arba)
cite.quote: Six of the suspects were charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with the machinegun and grenade attack last July on the Islamic College in Hebron in which three Arab students were killed and 33 were wounded.

cite.claim: and had planned to blow up the Dome of the Rock
cite.quote: others with conspiring to blow up the El Aksa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, two of the holiest shrines of Islam, on the Temple Mount in East Jerusalem.

cite.claim: neutrality: casualties of the Islamic College attack
cite.quote: Three Arab students were killed and 30 injured today in Hebron

affected_populations.note: Islamic College, Hebron, July 1983: three students killed and 30 injured (JTA); other reports give 33 wounded.
Two West Bank Arab mayors maimed by car bombs in June 1980 (JTA).
The bombs planted on Arab buses in East Jerusalem in April 1984 were defused after the arrests.

title: 1984 election and the rotation government
summary: The Alignment won 44 seats and Likud 41 on 23 July 1984; neither bloc could form a government. A national unity government was formed on 13 September 1984 with Shimon Peres as prime minister for two years and Yitzhak Shamir for the next two, and Yitzhak Rabin as defence minister throughout.

choices.label: Form a national unity government with a rotating premiership
choices.note: Peres for two years, then Shamir.

cite.claim: Peres and Shamir both needed the national unity arrangement
cite.quote: Second, both Peres and Shamir, as individuals, needed something like the “national unity” arrangement to preserve their own standing as leaders of their respective parties

choices.label: Form a narrow Likud-led government
choices.note: Likud's attempt, blocked when Ezer Weizman (Yahad) refused to join it despite Ariel Sharon's pressure.

cite.claim: Weizman's move blocked a narrow Likud government
cite.quote: When Weizman decided to form a political faction together with the Alignment, he was in fact blocking the Likud’s chances of forming a narrow- based government.

cite.claim: date 1984-07-23: the Alignment won 44 seats and Likud 41
cite.quote: Elections for the 11th Knesset 23.7.1984 ... Alignment 724,074 44 34.9 ... Likud 661,302 41 31.9

cite.claim: neither bloc could form a government; a national unity government with rotating premiership (Peres two years, then Shamir), Rabin defence minister throughout
cite.quote: the political system entered a state of numerical deadlock. ... a national unity government that operated on the basis of a rotation in the premiership. For first two years Shimon Peres would serve as Prime Minister and Yitzhak Shamir as Foreign Minister, and then they would switch positions. ... including Yitzhak Rabin as Minster of Defense.

cite.claim: the national unity government was formed on 13 September 1984
cite.quote: Government 21 13/09/1984 - 20/10/1986 Ministers Faction ** Prime Minister Shimon Peres 13/09/1984 - 20/10/1986 Alignment ... Minister of Defense Yitzhak Rabin 13/09/1984 - 20/10/1986 Alignment

cite.claim: choices (narrow Alignment-led / narrow Likud-led coalition) were genuinely attempted options amid deadlock
cite.quote: After Yahad (a list headed by Ezer Weizman) decided to align itself with the Alignment ... religious parties declared their allegiance to the Likud, the political system entered a state of numerical deadlock.

consequences.note: History took its course: the election of 23 July 1984 is held on its date and Shimon Peres becomes prime minister in September. Your cabinet formed a narrow Labor-led coalition instead of the rotation, so in your Israel the government lives on a fragile majority (Cohesion -1) and has no unity-government cover for hard economic measures; the game's later government rails (the change of prime minister in October 1986) still follow history's calendar.

title: Operation Moses
summary: Between 21 November 1984 and 5 January 1985 some 7,600 Ethiopian Jews who had trekked to refugee camps in Sudan were airlifted to Israel on dozens of night flights over 45 days. Reports in January 1985, quoting Sudanese officials and relief workers, said at least 2,000 Ethiopian Jews had died in the Sudanese camps, including nearly 1,800 of 7,000 at the Umm Rekuba camp. The airlift stopped after it became public; according to President Weizman, the United States also brought about 600 Jews out of the Sudanese camps in cargo planes.

cite.claim: date 1984-11-21 to 1985-01-05: about 8,000 Ethiopian Jews who had trekked to camps in Sudan were airlifted to Israel (places: abroad)
cite.quote: During Operation Moses, some 7,600 Ethiopian immigrants were flown to Israel on dozens of night flights from Sudan during a 45-day period.

cite.claim: the airlift stopped after it became public
cite.quote: The Jewish Agency confirmed today that the airlift of Ethiopian Jews to Israel via Sudan has been halted, apparently because it was prematurely disclosed

cite.claim: about 7,600 airlifted over 45 days
cite.quote: During Operation Moses, some 7,600 Ethiopian immigrants were flown to Israel on dozens of night flights from Sudan during a 45-day period.

cite.claim: the United States brought about 600 Jews out of the Sudanese camps (Weizman)
cite.quote: President Ezer Weizman said that friendly governments had assisted in carrying out the 1984 operation, including the United States, which brought 600 Jews from the refugee campus of Sudan in cargo planes.

cite.claim: reports said at least 2,000 Ethiopian Jews died in the Sudanese camps
cite.quote: Israeli and American Jewish officials active on behalf of Ethiopian Jewry had no comment today on reports over the weekend that at least 2,000 Ethiopian Jews have died in refugee camps in the eastern Sudan since they began to flee their homeland last spring.

cite.claim: nearly 1,800 of 7,000 died at Umm Rekuba; reports quoted Sudanese officials and relief workers
cite.quote: The reports, carried in The New York Times, quoted Sudanese officials and relief workers as estimating that beyond the hundreds who have perished in the Sudan, perhaps 2,000 more are stranded in the Sudan ... The report in the Times, from Gedaref, the Sudan, said that at one camp, Umm Rekuba, nearly 1,800 of the 7,000 Ethiopian Jews who arrived last year died there,

consequences.note: History took its course: the airlift from Sudan begins on 21 November 1984 on the game's calendar. Your cabinet had pressed publicly for a faster rescue, so in your Israel the operation is news from the start: the world's attention brings some standing (+1), and Ethiopia and Sudan harden, as your choice's lasting terms on growth show. The war had cost 654 Israeli soldiers and other security personnel dead and nearly 6,000 wounded. The zone's Lebanese residents lived under the control of the SLA and the IDF, and human-rights groups documented shelling of villages around it.

title: Economic Stabilization Plan
summary: With inflation running at several hundred percent a year (380.75% in the twelve months to June 1985), the unity government adopted an emergency stabilisation plan on 1 July 1985: an 18.8 percent devaluation that set the shekel at 1,500 to the dollar, deep subsidy and budget cuts, a three-month freeze on prices, wages and salaries, and a wage agreement with the Histadrut; in July the government printed no new money. title: New Israeli shekel introduced

title: Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif killings
summary: On 8 October 1990 clashes broke out on the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif amid tension over a planned 'Temple Mount Faithful' cornerstone ceremony that the High Court had refused; worshippers threw stones onto the Western Wall plaza and Israeli police fired tear gas, rubber bullets and live ammunition. According to the UN Secretary-General, reports varied between 17 and 21 Palestinians killed and more than 150 wounded by Israeli security forces, while more than 20 Israeli civilians and police were wounded; B'Tselem counted at least 17 Palestinians shot dead on the Mount. summary: After Hezbollah attacks on Israeli forces and rocket fire on northern Israel, the IDF carried out a week-long air and artillery campaign in south Lebanon. HRW counted some 120 Lebanese civilians killed and close to 500 injured; in Israel two civilians were killed, both in Kiryat Shmona, and 24 injured by Hezbollah rockets, and about half of Kiryat Shmona's residents left the town during the week. Hezbollah fighter deaths are disputed: Hezbollah later told HRW that seventeen of its fighters were killed, the IDF estimated fifty to eighty guerrillas killed, and Lebanese prime minister Hariri said eight. cite.claim: Week-long air and artillery campaign in south Lebanon (place south_lebanon)
cite.quote: Attacks by Israeli helicopter gunships, fighter jets and artillery were reported throughout southern Lebanon and the western Beqa' during the late afternoon and evening of Sunday, July 25, and throughout the night.

cite.claim: IDF warned civilians in the south to leave
cite.quote: During the first stage, residents of southern Lebanon were warned that they were in danger and should leave their homes

cite.claim: Some 300,000 people displaced for about a week
cite.quote: an assault which also temporarily displaced some 300,000 Lebanese villagers and Palestinian refugees.

cite.claim: A US-brokered understanding ended it on 31 July
cite.quote: Saturday, July 31, 1993, a cease-fire brokered by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher came into effect at 6:00 p.m., putting an end to hostilities.

cite.claim: Neutrality: Israeli casualties omitted
cite.quote: In Israel, two civilians were killed and twenty-four injured in retaliatory Hizballah rocket attacks.

cite.quote: the Israeli government's stated objective during Operation Accountability was to foment a refugee flow in order to put pressure on the Lebanese government to rein in Hizballah

cite.claim: Refugee flow aimed toward Beirut
cite.quote: The operation was also designed to create a refugee flow in the direction of Beirut so as to put pressure on the central government to rein in the guerrillas.

cite.claim: US-brokered understanding took effect 31 July 1993
cite.quote: brokered by the United States, that went into effect on July 31, 1993, as part of the cease-fire arrangement

cite.claim: Katyusha attack on Kiryat Shmona killed two civilians (place kiryat_shmona)
cite.quote: That evening, a Katyusha attack on Kiryat Shemona, a town of 15,000 in northern Israel, killed two Israeli civilians and wounded eight others

cite.claim: HRW 2007 restates the toll
cite.quote: Israeli operations resulted in the deaths of some 120 Lebanese civilians, injured close to 500, and temporarily drove an estimated 300,000 villagers and Palestinian refugees from their homes.

cite.quote: The two deaths occurred in separate rocket attacks on Sunday evening.

cite.claim: Hezbollah's own count: seventeen of its fighters killed (as of Oct 1993 interview)
cite.quote: Hizballah later claimed that seventeen of its fighters were killed during the week of July 25

cite.quote: stated that the IDF estimated that between fifty and eighty guerillas had been killed as a result of the military action

cite.claim: Lebanese PM Hariri: one soldier, eight Hezbollah fighters, 118 civilians killed
cite.quote: Lebanese prime minister Rafiq Hariri claimed that one Lebanese soldier, eight Hizballah fighters, and 118 civilians were killed

affected_populations.note: HRW: 'some 120' killed, 'close to 500' injured; some 300,000 villagers and Palestinian refugees temporarily displaced

Figures conflict and are partisan. Hezbollah (to HRW, interview of 20 Oct 1993): seventeen of its fighters killed during the week of 25 July; IDF (Col. Ben-Ari to HRW, 18 May 1994): between fifty and eighty guerrillas killed; Lebanese PM Hariri (Washington Post, 1 Aug 1993): eight Hezbollah fighters killed.
HRW counts Palestinian refugees among the ~300,000 displaced without a separate figure

title: Oslo Accords: Declaration of Principles
summary: After secret talks in Norway, Israel and the PLO, which had exchanged letters of recognition, signed the Declaration of Principles on the White House lawn. It provided for an elected Palestinian interim self-government in the West Bank and Gaza for a transitional period of up to five years, with permanent-status issues (Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, borders) left to later negotiation.

choices.label: Recognise the PLO and sign the Declaration of Principles
choices.note: The Rabin government signed the accord with the PLO in Washington; the Knesset approved it 61-50.

cite.claim: Knesset approved the Israel-PLO accord 61-50
cite.quote: the Knesset approved by a vote of 61-50 the accord signed last week in Washington by Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.

cite.claim: Rabin welcomed the margin and moved to implement
cite.quote: Rabin said after the vote that he was satisfied with the margin of victory and that it gave the government the confidence it needs to begin implementing the agreement.

choices.label: Reject the accord with the PLO
choices.note: The position of the Likud opposition: its leader Benjamin Netanyahu called on the party to stand firm against the accord.

cite.claim: Netanyahu urged Likud to stand firm against the accord
cite.quote: Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the opposition Likud party, had called on his party to stand firm against the accord

cite.claim: Date: signed 13 September 1993 in Washington (place washington)
cite.quote: DONE at Washington, D.C., this thirteenth day of September 1993.

cite.claim: Signed on the White House lawn
cite.quote: signed a Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements, commonly referred to as the “Oslo Accord,” at the White House.

cite.claim: After secret talks in Norway (place oslo)
cite.quote: U.S. officials were briefed on secret negotiations that the Israelis and Palestinians had begun in Oslo in December 1992

cite.claim: Israel and the PLO had exchanged letters of recognition
cite.quote: Israel accepted the PLO as the representative of the Palestinians, and the PLO renounced terrorism and recognized Israel’s right to exist in peace.

cite.claim: Provided for an elected Palestinian interim self-government in the West Bank and Gaza for a transitional period of up to five years
cite.quote: to establish a Palestinian Interim Self-Government Authority, the elected Council (the "Council"), for the Palestinian people in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, for a transitional period not exceeding five years

cite.claim: Permanent-status issues (Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, borders) left to later negotiation
cite.quote: It is understood that these negotiations shall cover remaining issues, including: Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security arrangements, borders, relations and cooperation with other neighbours

cite.claim: Choice 'Recognise the PLO and sign' was the historical decision of Rabin's government
cite.quote: On September 13, 1993, Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) Negotiator Mahmoud Abbas signed a Declaration of Principles

cite.claim: Choice 'Keep to the Madrid-format Washington talks without the PLO' was the existing official track (Jordanian-Palestinian delegation), stalled by 1993
cite.quote: Yet by 1993, the Washington talks had become deadlocked and were overtaken by secret Israeli-Palestinian and Israeli-Jordanian negotiations

consequences.note: Your cabinet stayed with the Washington talks and the Syrian track: without the Norway channel there is no Israel-PLO Declaration of Principles in September 1993, no mutual recognition and no peace dividend; the PLO stays outside the talks. In history Israel and the PLO signed the Declaration on the White House lawn on 13 September 1993.

title: Cave of the Patriarchs massacre
summary: On Purim, 25 February 1994, Baruch Goldstein, a physician from Kiryat Arba and Kach activist, opened fire on Muslim worshippers at prayer in the Ibrahimi Mosque/Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, killing 29 and injuring 129 (Israel State Archives) before he was overpowered and killed. Riots followed in the territories and East Jerusalem in which more Palestinians were killed and wounded by Israeli soldiers; the army said 3 more people were trampled in the mosque and 5 Palestinians were killed by soldiers in Hebron street battles. The government appointed a commission of inquiry headed by Supreme Court President Meir Shamgar; a preliminary army finding said Goldstein acted alone.

cite.claim: Date: 25 February 1994, on Purim
cite.quote: On Friday, February 25, 1994 (which was also the Jewish holiday of Purim) at 5:30 a.m.

cite.claim: Baruch Goldstein, a physician from Kiryat Arba and Kach activist (place kiryat_arba)
cite.quote: Baruch Goldstein, a physician from Kiryat Arba and an activist in the extremist Kach movement founded by Meir Kahane

cite.claim: Opened fire on Muslim worshippers at prayer in the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron (place hebron)
cite.quote: entered the Hall of Yitzhak in the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron and opened fire with a machine gun on the Muslim worshippers who were marking the month of Ramadan.

cite.claim: Killing 29 and wounding about 125-129
cite.quote: A total of 29 people praying in the Cave were killed in the incident and 129 were injured.

cite.claim: He was overpowered and killed
cite.quote: While Goldstein was trying to change the cartridge, one of the worshippers attacked and disarmed him. He was then attacked by other worshippers and killed.

cite.claim: The government appointed the Shamgar Commission
cite.quote: The commission of inquiry was headed by Supreme Court President Meir Shamgar

cite.claim: Neutrality: Palestinians killed by the IDF in the riots that followed are omitted
cite.quote: Serious riots broke out in the territories and in East Jerusalem, in which more people were killed and wounded by IDF soldiers.

cite.claim: 29 killed and 129 injured
cite.quote: A total of 29 people praying in the Cave were killed in the incident and 129 were injured.

cite.claim: Goldstein disarmed and killed by worshippers
cite.quote: one of the worshippers attacked and disarmed him. He was then attacked by other worshippers and killed.

cite.claim: Riots followed; more killed and wounded by IDF soldiers
cite.quote: Serious riots broke out in the territories and in East Jerusalem, in which more people were killed and wounded by IDF soldiers.

cite.claim: Commission headed by Shamgar
cite.quote: The commission of inquiry was headed by Supreme Court President Meir Shamgar

cite.claim: Army: 29 killed by Goldstein; 3 trampled
cite.quote: Dr. Goldstein killed 29 Palestinians, the general said. In addition, he said, 3 people were trampled to death as worshipers stampeded

cite.claim: 5 Palestinians later killed by soldiers in Hebron
cite.quote: 5 Palestinians were later killed by soldiers in street battles in other parts of Hebron

cite.claim: Preliminary army finding: Goldstein acted alone
cite.quote: which is based on a preliminary army finding that Dr. Goldstein acted alone

affected_populations.note: Israel State Archives: 29 killed and 129 injured in the mosque; Israeli army (NYT 9 Mar 1994): 3 more trampled and 5 killed by soldiers in Hebron street battles. Further deaths in riots elsewhere not quantified here
No Israeli victims reported; the attacker himself was disarmed and killed by worshippers

title: Gaza–Jericho Agreement (Cairo)
summary: Rabin and Arafat signed in Cairo the agreement implementing the first stage of Oslo: Israeli forces withdrew from most of the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area within weeks, and authority there passed to the new Palestinian Authority, with an annexed protocol on economic relations (Paris Protocol). Israeli settlements and military locations in Gaza remained under Israeli control.

cite.claim: Rabin and Arafat signed the agreement in Cairo (place cairo), 4 May 1994
cite.quote: Mr. Rabin accepted the changes and added his signature, bringing relieved applause from 1,500 dignitaries and journalists gathered in a conference center on the edge of Cairo.

cite.claim: Agreement implementing the first stage of Oslo
cite.quote: The September accord provides for the initial phase of a five-year interim period of limited Palestinian self-rule, to start upon the Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho.

cite.claim: Israeli forces withdrew from most of the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area within weeks (places gaza_city, khan_yunis, rafah, jericho)
cite.quote: Mr. Arafat had asked the Israelis to delay their total pullback for the 21 days allowed in the accord because the Palestinians were not ready to take over.

cite.claim: Authority passed to the new Palestinian Authority
cite.quote: The World Bank and many countries, including the United States, are committed to helping the Palestinian authority, as it is called, to survive.

cite.claim: With an annexed protocol on economic relations (Paris Protocol)
cite.quote: On May 4, the Cairo Agreement was signed between Israel and the PLO, establishing the Palestinian Authority in the Gaza Strip and Jericho. Shortly before that, an agreement that regulated economic relations between Israel and the PA (see the publication on the Cairo agreement) was signed in Paris

cite.claim: Israeli settlements and military locations in Gaza remained under Israeli control
cite.quote: Israeli troops are to remain at the Rafah border crossing and at Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip

consequences.note: History took its course on the map: Palestinian self-rule in Gaza and Jericho (the Cairo agreement of 4 May 1994) still appears on its date, although your cabinet never opened the Oslo channel. The agreement's diplomatic gains do not apply to you; your Washington-track terms do.

title: Nobel Peace Prize to Rabin, Peres and Arafat
title_he: פרס נובל לשלום לרבין, פרס וערפאת
summary: The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 1994 Peace Prize jointly to Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat for their efforts to create peace in the Middle East; the prize was presented in Oslo on 10 December 1994.

title: Dizengoff Street bus bombing
summary: A Hamas suicide bomber blew up a No. 5 Dan bus on Dizengoff Street in Tel Aviv on 19 October 1994, killing 22 people (21 Israelis and a Dutch national) and injuring 48; at the time it was the deadliest suicide bombing in Israel. Afterwards the army sealed off Gaza and the West Bank, keeping Palestinian labourers from their jobs in Israel.

cite.quote: At approximately 9:00 AM on October 19, 1994, as the bus was slowing down for a stop 100 meters north of Dizengoff Square, al-Souwi detonated the bomb

cite.quote: a bomb exploded on a commuter bus travelling in rush hour traffic near Dizengoff Square in the heart of Tel Aviv ... The bus, Dan Liens No. 5, was completely destroyed

cite.claim: A Hamas suicide bomber
cite.quote: The Palestinian terrorist organization Hamas claimed responsibility for this attack

cite.claim: Killing 22 people (21 Israelis and a Dutch national)
cite.quote: al-Souwi detonated the bomb, killing 21 Israelis and one Dutch national.

cite.claim: Injuring dozens
cite.quote: The bomb, which weighed approximately 10 kilograms, killed 22 people and injured 48.

cite.claim: At the time it was the deadliest suicide bombing in Israel
cite.quote: At the time of the attack, it was the deadliest in Israeli history.

cite.claim: 21 Israelis and one Dutch national killed
cite.quote: al-Souwi detonated the bomb, killing 21 Israelis and one Dutch national.

cite.quote: The Palestinian terrorist organization Hamas claimed responsibility for this attack

cite.quote: At the time of the attack, it was the deadliest in Israeli history.

cite.claim: Early report: at least 20 killed, 48 wounded
cite.quote: killing at least 20 people and wounding 48 others in one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in Israeli history.

cite.quote: the army sealed off Gaza and the West Bank in the hope of improving Israelis' sense of security but at the same time keeping Palestinian laborers from reaching jobs.
