title: Peace treaty with Jordan
summary: Prime ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Abdelsalam al-Majali signed the Israel–Jordan Treaty of Peace at the Arava/Araba crossing north of Eilat, witnessed by the United States and Russia, ending the state of war, fixing the international border and setting water-sharing arrangements for the Jordan and Yarmuk rivers.

cite.claim: Date: signed 26 October 1994
cite.quote: Done at the Arava/Araba Crossing Point this day Heshvan 21st, 5775, Jumada Al-Ula 21st, 1415 which corresponds to 26th October, 1994

cite.claim: Signed by prime ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Abdelsalam al-Majali
cite.quote: For the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdul Salam Majali Prime Minister ... Yitzhak Rabin ... Prime Minister

cite.claim: At the Arava/Araba crossing north of Eilat (places arava, eilat)
cite.quote: On October 26, 1994, the representatives of Israel and Jordan signed a peace treaty in a solemn ceremony near the Arava border crossing, north of Eilat, later known as the Yitzhak Rabin crossing.

cite.claim: Witnessed by the United States and Russia
cite.quote: signed by the two States at the Arava/Araba crossing-point on 26 October 1994, and witnessed by the United States of America and the Russian Federation.

cite.claim: Ending the state of war
cite.quote: Bearing in mind that in their Washington Declaration of 25th July, 1994, they declared the termination of the state of belligerency between them;

cite.claim: Fixing the international border
cite.quote: The international boundary between Israel and Jordan is delimited with reference to the boundary definition under the Mandate as is shown in Annex I(a)

cite.claim: Setting water-sharing arrangements for the Jordan and Yarmuk rivers
cite.quote: The Parties agree mutually to recognise the rightful allocations of both of them in Jordan River and Yarmouk River waters and Araba/Arava ground water

consequences.note: History took its course: Israel and Jordan sign their peace treaty on 26 October 1994 on the game's calendar. In history King Hussein moved to a public treaty only after the Israel-PLO Declaration of Principles; with no Oslo accord in your Israel, Amman signs more cautiously, so the treaty brings less standing (+2 instead of +4) and a cooler peace on the diplomacy screen.
consequences.relation_label: A treaty signed without a Palestinian track (your Israel)

title: Oslo II Interim Agreement
summary: Israel and the PLO signed the Interim Agreement in Washington, dividing the West Bank into Area A, where the Palestinian Council took over internal security and public order; Area B, where it took over public order for Palestinians while Israel kept overriding responsibility for security; and Area C, the rest of the West Bank, which was to be transferred gradually to Palestinian jurisdiction except for permanent-status issues. Israeli forces were to redeploy from the cities of Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Ramallah and Bethlehem and some 440 villages before the Palestinian elections the agreement provided for. The areas were drawn on the agreement's maps rather than given as shares in its text; after later redeployments Area A covered about 18% of the territory, Area B about 22% and Area C about 60% (Fanack).

cite.claim: Date: 28 September 1995; signed in Washington (place washington)
cite.quote: Done at Washington DC, this 28th day of September, 1995.

cite.claim: Signed by Israel and the PLO
cite.quote: (Signed) Yitzhak RABIN (Signed) Yasser ARAFAT

cite.claim: Divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C
cite.quote: The latter agreement divided the West Bank into separate areas under Israeli control, Palestinian control, and Israeli military responsibility with Palestinian civil administration, respectively.

cite.claim: Area A: full Palestinian civil and security control, including the main Palestinian towns
cite.quote: Area A covered the large Palestinian population areas, excluding East Jerusalem and Hebron, from which Israel was to withdraw. ... Here, both the civil and military administration was to be placed in the hands of a Palestinian Authority

cite.claim: Area B: Palestinian civil, joint (Israeli) security control
cite.quote: The B Areas were the villages and their direct surroundings; 21.8 percent. Here, the civil administration was in the hands of the PNA, whereas the military administration remained under Israel’s control.

cite.claim: After later redeployments Area A reached about 18%
cite.quote: After carrying through a few modifications, these covered 18.2 percent of the total territory.

cite.claim: Provided for Palestinian elections
cite.quote: The elections shall be called by the Chairman of the Palestinian Authority immediately following the signing of this Agreement to take place at the earliest

cite.claim: Agreement text defines Area A and B by map and Area C as the rest of the West Bank, to be gradually transferred
cite.quote: a. "Area A" means the populated areas delineated by a red line and shaded in brown on attached map No. 1 ; b. "Area B" means the populated areas delineated by a red line and shaded in yellow on attached map No. 1 , and the built-up area of the hamlets listed in Appendix 6 to Annex I , and c. "Area C" means areas of the West Bank outside Areas A and B, which, except for the issues that will be negotiated in the permanent status negotiations, will be gradually transferred to Palestinian jurisdiction in accordance with this Agreement.

cite.claim: Area A: Council assumes internal security and public order
cite.quote: The Council will, upon completion of the redeployment of Israeli military forces in each district, as set out in Appendix 1 to Annex I , assume the powers and responsibilities for internal security and public order in Area A in that district.

cite.claim: Area B: Council public order for Palestinians; Israel overriding security responsibility
cite.quote: Israel will transfer to the Council and the Council will assume responsibility for public order for Palestinians. Israel shall have the overriding responsibility for security for the purpose of protecting Israelis and confronting the threat of terrorism.

cite.claim: Redeployment from Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Ramallah, Bethlehem and some 440 villages before elections (places)
cite.quote: Redeployment of Israeli security forces from the cities of Jenin , Nablus , Tulkarm , Qalqilyah, Ramallah , and Bethlehem , as well as some 440 villages, before elections were to be held

cite.claim: Area C about 60% (Fanack)
cite.quote: In the C Areas (thinly populated areas where there were also Jewish settlements and Israeli military bases; 60 percent), both the civil and the military administration remained in Israeli hands.

consequences.note: History took its course on the map: the West Bank cities pass to the Palestinian Council on the dates of the Oslo II agreement (28 September 1995), although your cabinet never opened the Oslo channel and asked no Oslo II question. Its diplomatic gains do not apply to you; your Washington-track terms do.

title: Assassination of Yitzhak Rabin
summary: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead by Yigal Amir, a Jewish Israeli opponent of the Oslo process, as he left a peace rally at Kings of Israel Square in Tel Aviv; a security guard, Yoram Rubin, was slightly wounded. Shimon Peres succeeded him. Amir was sentenced to life imprisonment plus six years for wounding Rubin, and his brother Hagai was convicted of conspiracy to murder Rabin. The Shamgar Commission's final report (28 March 1996) criticised the Shin Bet for putting the prime minister at risk and ignoring threats from Jewish extremists.

title: Mizrahi Bank ruling – 'constitutional revolution'
summary: In United Mizrahi Bank v. Migdal Cooperative Village, a nine-justice Supreme Court panel led by Aharon Barak held that the 1992 Basic Laws have constitutional status and that courts may set aside ordinary legislation conflicting with them, establishing judicial review of Knesset laws. Supporters and critics alike call it the 'constitutional revolution'.

cite.claim: Date: 9 November 1995
cite.quote: November 9, 1995

cite.claim: Case: United Mizrahi Bank v. Migdal Cooperative Village (CA 6821/93)
cite.quote: CA 6821/93 concerned a suit brought by the appellant in the District Court against the respondents who had guaranteed the debt of the Cooperative Agricultural Fund Ltd.

cite.claim: Nine-justice Supreme Court panel led by Aharon Barak
cite.quote: Each of the nine judges wrote a separate opinion. The primary approach of the Court is set out in the opinion of President Barak.

cite.claim: Held that the 1992 Basic Laws have constitutional (supra-legislative) status
cite.quote: The Knesset has used its constituent authority to endow a number of legally protected human rights with constitutional supra-legislative status.

cite.claim: Courts may set aside ordinary legislation conflicting with them (judicial review)
cite.quote: The failure of a regular law to meet those requirements renders it unconstitutional. Such a law is constitutionally flawed and the Court may declare it void.

cite.claim: Called the 'constitutional revolution'
cite.quote: A. The constitutional revolution in human rights 1. The constitutional revolution occurred in the Knesset in March 1992.

title: Wave of suicide bombings in Jerusalem, Ashkelon and Tel Aviv
summary: In nine days Hamas suicide bombings killed about 60 people: 26 on Jerusalem bus 18 and one at an Ashkelon junction on 25 February, 19 on another bus 18 on 3 March, and 13–14 at Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Center on 4 March (UN tally 61; the US State Department gives 65, including three US citizens). Hamas presented them as revenge for Israel's January killing of bomb-maker Yahya Ayyash. Israel closed the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring some 22,000 Gaza workers from jobs in Israel. Leaders of 27 (UN count) to 29 (US State Department) countries met at a 'Summit of the Peacemakers' in Sharm el-Sheikh on 13 March.

cite.claim: About 60 killed in nine days (UN tally 61)
cite.quote: bringing the nine-day death toll to 61.

cite.claim: Hamas suicide bombings

cite.claim: Leaders of 29 countries met at the 'Summit of the Peacemakers' in Sharm el-Sheikh on 13 March

title: Operation Grapes of Wrath and the Qana shelling
title_he: מבצע ענבי זעם והפגזת כפר קנא
summary: Following Hezbollah rocket fire on northern Israel, the IDF launched a 17-day air and artillery campaign in Lebanon (11–27 April); Human Rights Watch writes that, as in 1993, its warnings were designed in part to displace upwards of 400,000 Lebanese civilians. On 18 April Israeli shells struck the UNIFIL Fijian battalion compound at Qana, where about 800 civilians sheltered, killing more than 100. A UN military adviser found it unlikely that the shelling resulted from technical or procedural error; the IDF attributed it to operational mistakes. Over the whole operation HRW counted some 154 Lebanese civilians killed and 351 injured; Hezbollah fired 639 Katyusha rockets into Israel, injuring 62 Israeli civilians and killing none (IDF figures). It ended with the Israel–Lebanon Ceasefire Understanding of 26 April.

summary: President Clinton hosted Barak and Arafat at Camp David for final-status talks from 11 to 24 July 2000 (Jewish Virtual Library dates). Participants disagree about responsibility: US envoy Dennis Ross and Israeli negotiator Shlomo Ben-Ami largely blamed Arafat, while US negotiator Robert Malley and co-author Hussein Agha attributed tactical errors to the Israelis and Americans as well as the Palestinians, and the Palestinian Authority's account held that Israel had offered only a fragmented state of disconnected cantons.

title: Second (Al-Aqsa) Intifada begins
summary: Opposition leader Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif on 28 September 2000 was followed the next day by protests in which Israeli police used lethal force, and by a spiral of uprising, armed attacks and suicide bombings, and Israeli military operations. The Mitchell Report found the visit did not cause the intifada but was poorly timed, and faulted both sides. title: October 2000 events: Arab citizens killed in protests
summary: In early October 2000 protests by Arab citizens in the Galilee and Wadi Ara, including blocked roads and stone-throwing, spread into clashes; police killed 13 Palestinian Arabs, 12 of them citizens of Israel and one a resident of Gaza, and more than 1,000 protesters were wounded. A Jewish citizen was also killed, and in a second wave of events retaliatory Jewish riots against Arabs broke out in several places. The Or Commission (report published in 2003) found police live and rubber-bullet fire unjustified and the use of snipers against police regulations; the police investigations unit decided in 2005 not to indict, and the attorney general closed the cases in 2007.

title: Rocket fire from Gaza on Sderot
summary: Early in the second intifada Palestinian armed groups in the Gaza Strip began firing home-made Qassam rockets and mortars at Sderot and nearby communities, and in 2008 also at Ashkelon and Netivot; Human Rights Watch dates the Qassam's development to late 2001 and its first attack on Israel to 5 March 2002, while its 2009 report counts rocket fire 'since 2001'. HRW counted 15 civilians inside Israel killed by rockets from 2001 to May 2009 and reported that thousands of people moved away from frequently targeted areas such as Sderot. The rockets also killed Palestinians: two Palestinian workers and a Chinese worker in a Gaza settlement in June 2005, at least two Palestinian civilians by mid-2007 when rockets fell short inside Gaza, and two girls in Gaza from late 2008.

title: Operation Defensive Shield
summary: Two days after the Netanya bombing Israel launched a major West Bank operation, entering Ramallah on 29 March, Tulkarm and Qalqilya on 1 April, Bethlehem on 2 April and Jenin and Nablus on 3 April. In the battle of Jenin refugee camp at least 52 Palestinians were killed—22 of them civilians according to Human Rights Watch, up to half according to the UN—and 23 Israeli soldiers; most accounts cited by the UN put the Palestinian dead in Nablus at 70–80, about 50 of them civilians. For the reoccupation of Palestinian areas from 1 March to 7 May 2002 the UN Secretary-General's report counted 497 Palestinians killed and 1,447 wounded, more than 17,000 people left homeless or in need of shelter repair and an estimated 1 million under round-the-clock curfews; Israel's Foreign Ministry said the IDF lost 30 soldiers in the operation. Palestinian officials' claims of a massacre of hundreds in Jenin were not borne out by HRW or the UN, though HRW documented unlawful killings and use of human shields. The IDF declared the operation over on 21 April.

title: Knesset passes the Tal Law on yeshiva-student deferrals
summary: On 23 July 2002 the Knesset voted 51-41 to approve the Tal Law, an effort to address the growing problem of Haredi men receiving exemptions from military service. The law followed a 1998 High Court ruling that the defence minister lacked the authority to grant sweeping exemptions to yeshiva students without explicit legislation, and the Tal Committee formed under Ehud Barak in 1999. For the first time it regulated the deferral of yeshiva students' service in law. In 2006 a nine-judge High Court panel declined to invalidate it despite its disproportionate impact on equality. Supporters of the exemption argue Torah study protects the state; critics, including the petitioners who challenged the law, argue it undermines equality in the burden of service.

summary: The state commission of inquiry headed by Justice Theodore Or into the October 2000 events, in which 12 Arab citizens of Israel, one Jewish citizen and one Gaza resident were killed, published its report. On 19 September 2007 Israel's Security Cabinet declared Gaza 'hostile territory', citing continued Qassam rocket fire on Sderot and other communities, and added restrictions on goods, fuel, electricity and movement; Israel cites rocket fire and weapons smuggling (including via tunnels), and a 2011 UN panel judged the separate naval blockade (January 2009) a legitimate security measure. title: Operation Cast Lead (Gaza War 2008–09)
summary: Israel launched a three-week air and ground offensive against Hamas in the Gaza Strip on 27 December 2008, which ended on 18 January 2009; Palestinian armed groups fired rockets at southern Israel during it. Palestinian deaths: the IDF's March 2009 figure is 1,166 (709 involved in hostilities, 295 uninvolved civilians, 162 undetermined); B'Tselem counted 1,387 (773 who did not take part in hostilities, including 320 minors; 330 combatants; 245 policemen per Ynet's report of B'Tselem's data, 248 in B'Tselem's own release); the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR) counted 1,434 (960 civilians, 239 police, 235 combatants, as reported by Ynet). The dispute centres partly on the police, whom PCHR counted as non-combatants and an Israeli think tank (ICT) said were often Hamas militants. Palestinian figures cited by the BBC give more than 5,300 injured; 55,000 people sheltered in UN schools at the height of the fighting and at least 66,000 had still not returned home a week after the ceasefire. Thirteen Israelis were killed according to B'Tselem as reported by Ynet: three civilians and a security officer by rocket fire, five soldiers in Gaza and four soldiers by friendly fire. The UN fact-finding mission led by Richard Goldstone, which Israel refused access, reported in September 2009 strong evidence of war crimes and crimes against humanity. On 1 April 2011 Goldstone wrote in the Washington Post that 'If I had known then what I know now, the Goldstone Report would have been a different document', adding that the Israeli investigations would probably have influenced the mission's findings about intentionality and war crimes (as quoted by the Jewish Virtual Library).

A Jewish Week editorial at the time put the number of exempted yeshiva students at about 70,000, against 400 in 1948. Defence Minister Ehud Barak welcomed the decision.

title: Operation Protective Edge (2014 Gaza war)
summary: War between Israel and Hamas and other Gaza groups from 7 July 2014 (UN Commission of Inquiry dating; Israel dates Operation Protective Edge from 8 July) to 26 August 2014, 51 days counted from 7 July. Gaza groups fired 4,881 rockets and 1,753 mortars toward Israel; on 17 July Israel launched a ground operation that it said targeted cross-border tunnels, and the IDF found 32 tunnels, 14 of them extending into Israel. The UN Commission of Inquiry counted 2,251 Palestinians killed, including 1,462 civilians (551 children), and 11,231 injured; the IDF's preliminary analysis counted 2,125 dead, at least 936 of them militants and 761 civilians. At the height of hostilities about 500,000 people in Gaza (28% of the population) were displaced, and 18,000 housing units were destroyed or damaged (OCHA). 67 Israeli soldiers and 6 civilians in Israel were killed and up to 1,600 Israelis injured; according to sources cited by OCHA, as many as 70% of the roughly 40,000 residents of communities near Gaza left their homes. An Egyptian-brokered open-ended ceasefire began on 26 Aug 2014.

title: Stabbing attack at the Jerusalem Pride parade; Shira Banki dies

title: March-May 2022 attack wave in Israel and Operation Break the Wave

Israeli authorities, as reported by the US State Department, counted 21 Israelis killed from March to May; the attackers included Arab citizens of Israel, whom the authorities described in one case as inspired by ISIS, and Palestinians from the West Bank. Prime Minister Bennett described the attacks as a wave of terrorism, and the IDF launched Operation Break the Wave, with almost daily raids in the West Bank for the rest of the year. According to figures the UN gave the Washington Post, Israeli security forces killed 146 Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 2022 through 19 December, against 75 in 2021; that figure covers the whole year and is not broken down for March to May.

title: Operation Breaking Dawn: Israel-Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighting in Gaza
summary: On 5 August 2022 Israel struck Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) targets in Gaza, killing its northern Gaza commander Tayseer Jabari, in what Israel said was a pre-emptive operation against an imminent attack; Khaled Mansour was killed in Rafah on 7 August. PIJ and other groups fired roughly 1,100 rockets and projectiles at Israel, about 200 of which fell short inside Gaza according to Israeli sources. A ceasefire brokered by Egypt and the UN took effect at 23:30 on 7 August. The UN human rights office confirmed 48 Palestinians killed including 17 children; OCHA's earlier verified count was 46; the Gaza health ministry figure reported by the Israeli Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center was 44. Israel and Palestinian sources dispute who caused some deaths: the Israeli army says an explosion in Jabalia that killed six people, including four children, was caused by a misfired Palestinian rocket, while Palestinian sources attribute it to an Israeli airstrike. Magen David Adom took 47 Israelis to hospital (Israeli authorities reported 70 injured); the US State Department reported no Israeli casualties from the rocket fire.

affected_populations.note: OHCHR 48 killed incl. 17 children (11 Aug 2022); OCHA verified 46 incl. 15 children as of 8 Aug; Gaza health ministry as reported by ITIC: 44 killed, 360 wounded. Israel says some deaths, especially of children, were caused by Palestinian rocket misfires; Palestinian sources attribute them to Israeli strikes. Includes PIJ members (Jerusalem Brigades said 12 operatives killed, per ITIC).

Magen David Adom evacuated 47 to hospital; Israeli authorities reported 70 injured (OCHA). US State Dept reports no Israeli casualties from rocket fire (intercepted or fell in open areas); the breakdown of the injuries is not given in the sources.

title: Huwara shooting and settler rampage
summary: On 26 February 2023 a Palestinian gunman shot dead two Israeli brothers from Har Bracha, Hillel Yaniv (22) and Yagel Yaniv (20), as they drove on Road 60 through Huwara south of Nablus. That night hundreds of settlers (a local Palestinian official estimated about 400) attacked Huwara and nearby villages: OCHA recorded at least 37 inhabited houses damaged, 55 private cars and 1,200 scrapped vehicles burned and eight households displaced. Sameh Aqtash, 37, was shot dead in Za'tara; OCHA says the fire came from either settlers or Israeli forces and his brother said soldiers fired; the Palestinian health ministry reported more than 100 injured, most from tear gas. According to Israeli forces, settlers also injured a soldier, and OCHA reported a firefighter injured when settlers attacked a fire truck. The IDF's regional commander called it a 'pogrom'; Prime Minister Netanyahu urged people not to take the law into their own hands, while Finance Minister Smotrich said on 1 March that Huwara 'needs to be wiped out'.
